newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS - Thais grapple with toughest economic crisis.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Thais grapple with toughest economic crisis.

text.p: Thailand is facing its toughest financial crisis in years as speculators attack its currency, its stock market hit new lows, and old economic and political wounds have reopened, analysts and economists said on Thursday.
As the Bank of Thailand this week repeatedly defended the baht through expensive multi-billion-dollar domestic and regional interventions, speculators hammered away gleefully.

Thai stocks hit a near eight-year low as turmoil over the baht and confusing signals from officials on economic policy, the budget deficit and the future of unelected Finance Minister Amnuay Virawan confused and worried players.

At 0809 GMT, the Thai stock index was down 19.98 points, or 3.50 percent, at 551.32. The baht was quoted at 25.520/720 to the dollar against 26.330/430 late on Wednesday, aided by central bank interventions.
Politicking within Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh's six-party coalition government saw a major partner work behind the scenes for Amnuay's removal.
Bitter divisions within three separate economic teams working for the finance minister, the prime minister and the major Chart Pattana Party also broke into the open this week.

"When an advisor of the prime minister attacks the finance minister, people will think the prime minister has no confidence in the head of his economic team," said Somjai Phagaphasvivat, a political scientist at Thammasat University.
"At a crucial time like this, when we have open differences of opinion from government, it makes investors lose confidence and has led to the problems we face today," he added.
Chavalit, however, has said he stands by Amnuay, who has stressed that he enjoys the premier's full support.
But the opposition Democrat Party pounced on the economic and political turmoil to speculate that the government may fall and fresh polls may be imminent.
"Looking at the way this government is running the country, a general election is forthcoming," said Sanan Kachornprasart, the Democrat Party's secretary general.

Most analysts do not expect the government, which took power in December, to fall so soon. But they warn that if coalition politicking gets out of hand, finance ministers are replaced quickly and the shaky economy slides further into lethargy, the administration could crumble.

Economists and analysts said Thailand, which in March ordered a revamp of its troubled, cash-strapped financial institutions and ailing property sector, was sailing into uncharted waters with its latest economic problems.

"We have entered into uncharted territory now, speculators and shorts are having a field day and Thailand is paying the ultimate price of not firmly putting its house in order," said the head of a U.S. investment bank who declined to be named.

Thailand's latest problems stem from high interest rates, used to defend the baht against speculative attacks, and their negative effect on the sluggish economy, which is expected to post about five percent growth this year -- the lowest in a decade, analysts said.
The rates, while successful in bringing in short-term capital inflows, have sparked liquidity crunches, dampened business and hurt the finance and property sectors badly.

"The critical question is the currency. What is going to happen to it? There is difficult tension between high short term baht rates and bringing them down to fit the economy," said Richard Henderson, head of research at KrungThai Thanakit Plc.

Although most analysts have ruled out a devaluation, which would be unacceptable politically and domestically, they believe that reform of the Thai currency system is imperative after recent heavy speculator attacks on the baht.

"If there is an adjustment of the currency system it will remove a structural constraint of high rates and give Thailand room to stabilise economic trouble spots faster," said the chief analyst at a foreign brokerage who declined to be named.
Otherwise, Thailand would have to continue deflating the economy and endure a couple of painful years before arriving at a recovery, he added.
